Calcium (Ca²⁺) plays an absolutely critical role in determining the structure, quantity, and functional quality of LDL receptors (LDLR). Without adequate levels of intracellular and extracellular calcium ions, these receptors lose their ability to fold correctly, bind cholesterol, and recycle, which directly leads to an impairment in clearing "bad" cholesterol from the blood.
Calcium affects LDL receptors in the following areas:

1. Receptor Quality and Structure (Proper Folding)

• Calcium cages: The ligand-binding domain of the LDL receptor consists of repeated sequences rich in cysteine (known as LR repeats). Each of these repeats features specific pockets that bind Ca²⁺ ions. Calcium acts as a physical skeleton or "glue" that stabilizes the 3D structure of the receptor.
• Effects of calcium deficiency: In a calcium-free environment, the receptor undergoes partial unfolding and loses its proper spatial conformation. Genetic mutations that destroy the calcium-binding sites in the LDLR are one of the main causes of familial hypercholesterolemia – the receptor becomes qualitatively defective, fails to recognize LDL particles, and gets trapped inside the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).

2. LDL Particle Binding Capacity (Quality of Action)

• Affinity for Apolipoproteins B and E: For a receptor located on the surface of a hepatocyte (liver cell) to capture a circulating LDL (or VLDL) particle, the presence of calcium is required. Ca²⁺ ions stabilize the negatively charged amino acids of the receptor, enabling a strong and specific bond with the positively charged ApoB-100 or ApoE proteins found on the surface of lipoproteins.

3. Receptor Quantity and Recycling (Availability on the Cell Surface)

• Release mechanism in endosomes: After the receptor-LDL complex enters the cell (endocytosis), the receptor must release its cholesterol cargo in order to return (recycle) to the cell surface. This process is triggered by two factors inside the endosome: an acidic pH and a drop in free calcium concentration.
• A low calcium level inside the endosome induces a deliberate change in the shape (unfolding) of the receptor, forcing the LDL particle to untie. Thanks to this, the free receptor returns to the cell membrane. Disruptions in calcium gradients prevent this process, reducing the pool of functional receptors on the cell surface.
• Cell differentiation: Local, high concentrations of extracellular calcium (e.g., in studies on keratinocytes or epithelial cells) stimulate cell differentiation, which naturally downregulates the expression (reduces the quantity) of LDL receptors in some peripheral tissues in favor of synthesizing their own structural proteins.
Summary of Relationships (Calcium Ca²⁺ vs. LDL Receptor):
🔹 RECEPTOR QUALITY (3D Structure)
• Ca²⁺ Impact: Critical. Calcium forms the structural core of the binding repeats. Without an adequate amount of Ca²⁺, the protein undergoes denaturation and misfolding.
🔹 QUALITY OF ACTION (LDL Binding)
• Ca²⁺ Impact: Essential. Ca²⁺ ions enable a strong, physical connection between the receptor and the apolipoproteins (ApoB/ApoE) on the surface of the LDL particle.
🔹 RECEPTOR QUANTITY (Availability on the Membrane)
• Ca²⁺ Impact: Regulatory. A deliberate drop in Ca²⁺ concentration inside the endosome triggers the release of the LDL cargo, allowing the receptor to safely recycle back to the cell surface.

top_comments.text:
Anita, cutting picanha is actually a little different than other steaks.  If you are going to cut "regular" steaks with it (like you are, it appears) then you want to cut the steaks WITH the grain.  Then, when you slice the cooked steak on your plate, you will be slicing ACROSS the grain and you will have very short fibers.

Cutting the initial steak against the grain like you did will result in longer muscle fibers in the piece that you put into your mouth.

If you care cutting pieces to put on skewers in a C-shape like they do in the Brazilian restaurants, then it will be sliced differently at the table.  In that case, you want to cut your initial steaks WITH the grain.

But yes, I wholeheartedly agree that this is a GREAT cut at a GREAT price.  In fact, I just had a 1.5-pound picanha steak yesterday with that big ol' fat cap.  🥰
